title: VPN data allowance
body: A VPN still uses your mobile connection. A successful tunnel does not demonstrate free mobile data or a free carrier package.

title: Read the server result
body: A server handshake and HTTPS check show that the tested tunnel worked from the test environment. Your SIM, signal and mobile plan still need their own test.

title: Protect private keys
body: A WireGuard private key is a credential. Keep configuration files private and avoid posting their contents in public support requests.

title: Public keys identify peers
body: WireGuard peers exchange public keys. A public key and a private key have different roles; never substitute one for the other.

title: Endpoint addresses
body: An endpoint tells WireGuard where a peer can be reached. Its location does not establish which mobile carrier supports a configuration.

title: Handshake timing
body: WireGuard establishes encrypted sessions when traffic is needed. A quiet connection can differ from a failed connection; check using actual traffic.

title: Keepalive purpose
body: Persistent keepalive can help a peer behind NAT remain reachable. It does not unlock a mobile package or change carrier billing.

title: Allowed IP routing
body: AllowedIPs helps determine what traffic belongs to a WireGuard peer. Review routing before importing an unfamiliar configuration.

title: Install official tools
body: Use the WireGuard installation documentation to find supported installation methods for your platform.

title: WireGuard on Android
body: WireGuard provides Android installation information. Review the app source and publisher before installing a VPN application.

title: WireGuard on Windows
body: The installation page links the Windows client. Download software through the official project rather than an unknown mirror.

title: WireGuard on Linux
body: WireGuard installation steps vary by Linux distribution. Follow the instructions for your own distribution.

title: WireGuard on macOS
body: The official installation page lists macOS options. A configuration still needs valid credentials and a reachable server.

title: Understand VPN scope
body: A VPN carries traffic through a tunnel to another network. It does not replace the internet connection used to reach that tunnel.

title: Review the provider
body: VPN protection depends partly on the service operating the exit server. Read the provider’s documentation before trusting a shared configuration.

title: HTTPS remains useful
body: Keep using HTTPS websites while connected to a VPN. A tunnel and website encryption protect different parts of the connection.

title: Check your plan separately
body: Check mobile data allowance with your carrier. VPN connection success alone is not billing evidence.

title: Use a clear test record
body: When reporting a cellular test, record the exact configuration hash, carrier, plan and time. A result for another file cannot verify yours.

title: Avoid command hooks
body: Inspect unfamiliar configuration files before importing them. Some command-line helpers support additional behavior beyond tunnel settings.

title: Route changes affect apps
body: Routing configuration determines which traffic uses the tunnel. Test the applications you actually intend to use.

title: Android VPN permission
body: Android requires user approval when an application prepares a VPN service. Read the permission prompt before allowing a new VPN app.

title: One Android VPN service
body: Android allows one active VPN service per user or profile. Starting a different service can replace the existing VPN connection.

title: Always-on VPN
body: Android supports always-on VPN settings. Review their behavior before relying on the tunnel for continuous connectivity.

title: Blocking without VPN
body: Android VPN settings can block connections without a VPN. Losing the tunnel can then affect internet access.

title: Android per-app routing
body: Android VPN applications can support app-specific routing. Check your app settings to understand which traffic uses the VPN.

title: VPN lifecycle
body: An Android VPN service must handle its connection lifecycle. Switching networks or stopping the service can affect an active tunnel.

title: Commit-pinned downloads
body: A Git commit identifier points to a specific revision. A branch name can move as the repository changes.

title: Read repository permission
body: Public visibility lets you view a repository, but permission to reuse material depends on its license and the author’s terms.

title: Report security privately
body: If you find exposed credentials in a project, use its documented security reporting process when available. Avoid copying secrets into public issues.

title: Inspect file history
body: Repository history helps you review how a file changed. A newer revision still needs fresh verification before it is trusted as working.

title: Follow source provenance
body: Keep the original source and revision alongside a download link. Provenance helps users understand exactly which published file was tested.

title: Revoke leaked credentials
body: Deleting a public copy is not enough after a credential leaks. Follow the provider’s process to revoke or replace affected credentials.
